Press Release:


Ticket to Mars
Why live on Earth when you can live on Mars? Strictly speaking, it’s not that simple. From extreme cold to an atmosphere so thin that skin and organs would rupture without a spacesuit and a continual bombardment of deadly solar radiation, Mars is hostile to human life. Yet NASA plans to send astronauts to the red planet and private company Mars One has volunteers who want to go there and never come back. Carte Blanche asks – is sending humans to Mars the most extraordinary thing that will happen this century?


Script:


TRANSCRIPT
Comments
download video: mp4


mars_astronaut_small.jpg
Woman
T-minus one minute.

Man
Engine start box go.

NARRATION
Sitting on top of that rocket is the craft that will take astronauts to Mars. For the first time, humanity will expand to another planet.

Man
5-4-3-2-1.

Dr Paul Marshall
We are on the path to Mars - that's what's exciting.

Dianne McGrath
This is the first humans will have been on another planet.

Bas Lansdorp
Going to Mars is the most exciting thing that will happen in the 21st century.

Man
And lift-off.

Dr Paul Marshall
So, you'll see new technologies develop and new economies emerge and, really, a new generation of space explorers will be defined through this process.

NARRATION
This is the first test flight of the Orion spacecraft which replaces the shuttles. It went into orbit around the earth.

Dr Paul Marshall
Well, it was a great day for Orion. The mission itself was a two-orbit mission. The second orbit projected up to 3,600 miles, the highest a human spacecraft has gone since Apollo 17 in 1972.

Man
The service panel jettisons...

NARRATION
And if you're excited by all this Mars talk, there's good news - these days NASA's not the only game in town. Private company Mars One has already advertised for astronauts to go to the red planet and never come back. Would anyone sign up for that?

Bas Lansdorp
Well, apparently so. We had more than 200,000 applications from people who said, 'I want to be on your first team.'

NARRATION
Here's just a selection. No astronaut experience necessary.

Woman
I am not a scientist.

Man
My name is M1-K0. I was 100,100 years ago on Mars.

Man 2
The time for mankind to live on Mars is now.

Woman 2
I wanna go to Mars 'cause it is the ultimate experience of a lifetime. I wanna achieve the best, I wanna do amazing things.

Woman 3
24. PhD student in astrophysics.

Man 2
Let's go to Mars.

Dr Graham Phillips
Mars One says, unlike NASA, they're going to use private money to get people to Mars. They also say they're going to get people there much sooner. In fact, 2027 is the date they're talking about at the moment. But the key difference is they'll do it much more cheaply, primarily because they're not bringing the astronauts back.

NARRATION
The shortlist of one-way astronauts is now down to 100, and Melburnian Dianne McGrath is on it.

Dianne McGrath
I was born the day before Neil Armstrong stepped on the moon.

NARRATION
Her drive to go to Mars is to offer humanity a fresh start.

Dianne McGrath
It's a chance to see, can we really show that we can survive on 100% renewable energy? What about our waste-management systems. We can't dig a big hole in the back of Mars and jump our waste there. So, I love the idea of, can we, on another planet, work out a way to manage our resources in such a way that we preserve the planet?

Dr Graham Phillips
But what about the one-way aspect of it? You're heading off and not coming back.

Dianne McGrath
Yeah. And maybe that's part of the adventure that I like in life. There are people out there that think, 'You're crazy, wanting to do this...'

Dr Graham Phillips
I'm sure there's a lot of people out there that think that.

Dianne McGrath
Oh, undoubtedly. And then I guess they get to meet me and then understand some of the motivations behind it about inspiring our youth of today.

NARRATION
Inspiring a new generation is one thing but Mars One's plans do sound very ambitious, perhaps a little crazy even.

Bas Lansdorp
There's always been people that wanted to go to new places, the frontier. For example, in 1900, if someone migrated to Australia, he probably had friends and family that said, 'Are you crazy?' The education system, the housing, the medical care in Australia is not as good as it is back in Europe back in 1900, and 'You're going there? Why are you going?'

NARRATION
But a one-way ticket to Mars? We asked a leading space engineer what he thought of Mars One's plans.

Professor Andrew Dempster
I think sending people to Mars is an interesting thing to think about. I think it's entirely possible to adapt to living on Mars. We need projects like Mars One in order to start this conversation.

NARRATION
Even NASA wasn't dismissive.

Dr Paul Marshall
In NASA, as a major initiative, we're very much encouraging the participation of private commercial enterprises in the exploration of space.

NARRATION
NASA, of course, are the only ones with a significant Mars budget at the moment though, and this is the official Orion mock-up used for design in astronaut training. There are two seats in it at the moment. Eventually, there will be four. But most noticeably, its shape is just a pod. Compare that to the space shuttle with its wings and almost aeroplane-like appearance. The reason for the difference is, unlike the shuttle, Orion will go into deep space, not just low-earth orbit, and so will travel at much greater speeds.

Dr Paul Marshall
A typical velocity in low-earth orbit is something around 17,500mph. To leave earth orbit, we have to be up closer to 25-30,000 mph. In those cases, you never take wings - you can't support the structures for that sort of thing.

NARRATION
A new launch rocket also has to be developed to get Orion to those high speeds.

Dr Paul Marshall
It's a much-faster regime, requiring a lot of energy to get out of what we call the 'gravity well' of earth or any other large planetary body.

NARRATION
And I'm guessing the new launch rocket was named by the engineers. It's called a Space Launch System.

Dr Paul Marshall
What it may lack in a name, actually is way made up for in power. It is going to be the largest rocket that we've ever employed to human space flight.

NARRATION
But there are still big technological challenges getting astronauts to Mars. Incredibly, we still don't even know how to land them on the red planet, despite having landed a lot of robotic craft there, starting with the Viking spacecraft in the 1970s. Now, NASA's come up with some innovative landing methods over the years, but weight is the key. This technique only worked because the Pathfinder rover inside was just a couple of hundred kilograms. To get the massive, almost one-tonne Curiosity down - the biggest rover ever landed - required a radically new method. Catalyst was at NASA for the landing in 2012, and stress levels were sky high, because the new landing technique required a lot of things to go right.

Dr Graham Phillips
We've got about 15 minutes to touchdown and the tension's really building.

NARRATION
The spacecraft hits Mars' upper atmosphere at 21,000km/h. It's first slowed by friction, protected by a heat shield. Next, a parachute's released. Then the retrorockets kick in. And finally, nylon cables lower the Curiosity to the surface.

Man
Touchdown confirmed...

(NASA engineers cheer)

Dr Graham Phillips
They've pulled it off. That was an incredibly difficult landing.

(Engineers cheer and applaud)

NARRATION
But even this risky method wouldn't work for getting humans down on Mars. Because their craft will be much heavier than even Curiosity.

Dr Graham Phillips
Here's the thing. For heavier craft, the atmosphere on Mars is too thin for parachutes to work - there just wouldn't be the time to slow the craft down. So, 'use retrorockets', you might say, like we did landing on the moon. Well, the trouble there is, unlike the moon, there is some atmosphere on Mars, and that causes turbulence in the retrorockets.

Dr Paul Marshall
Absolutely it is a major challenge, and you'll see some marked differences between what we did on the Curiosity lander or the Pathfinder landers before that, that the robotics were able to take some forces and things that the crew will not. So, you'll see some major differences.

NARRATION
Some form of retrorockets will be used, but it won't be plain sailing.

Dr Paul Marshall
Obviously it's the type of technology and function that we have addressed in the past, such the lunar landers that we had earlier.

NARRATION
If the mission and landing are successful, and the astronauts set foot on Mars, life will certainly be challenging. It appears like the Australian desert here, apart from the blue sunsets. But looks are deceiving. Temperatures are mostly below freezing. The atmosphere's so thin your skin and organs would rupture without a spacesuit. And this place is continually bombarded by deadly radiation. The radiation is a real issue. The Curiosity rover recently measured it meticulously. It's in the form of tiny, high-speed particles raining down from space. And spacesuits won't protect against it. One source of them is, well, chunks of the sun that are regularly belched into space. These are clouds of cancer-causing high-energy particles which, luckily, are deflected from earth by our planet's magnetic field. The beautiful aurorae are side effects of the process. But Mars has no protective magnetic field. When the sun belches a coronal mass ejection, as they're called, the astronauts will cop the full brunt. I caught up with the head of Mars One, visiting Melbourne, to find out about his plans for coping with the sun's ravages.

Bas Lansdorp
It's never going to be lethal dose - it's always going to be an increased risk, for example, for developing a tumour because of the radiation, which is why we will protect our people inside the habitat with a layer of soil - a layer of sand - on top of the habitat. So, inside the habitat they will be protected just about as well as we are here on earth.

NARRATION
A warning system for when the sun lets loose will have to be set up. We have them here.

Bas Lansdorp
On earth already, we know when a big solar flare is coming, and we have about 30 minutes of warning ahead of that.

NARRATION
Here, when the warning comes, we lower the power in our electricity grids. On Mars, the astronauts will drop what they're doing and head straight indoors. But there's more. Who would've thought that distant black holes and exploding stars would pose a risk too? They eject high-speed, cancer-causing particles to all corners of the galaxy, including Mars. To lower the risk from this continual rain of particles Bas says two hours a day outside the habitat would be a maximum.

Bas Lansdorp
People say, 'Oh, they can only go outside two hours per day!' But I think the average person in Australia probably doesn't get two hours per day outside. A lot of people are in their office, they walk to their car - one minute outside - they drive home, they walk to their front door - ten minutes outside - and that's it.

NARRATION
For Dianne, leaving family, friends and a partner behind will be the tough part, although she says they're all very supportive.

Dianne McGrath
We have a ten-year window - ten years when we can be physically in each other's lives - but then after that, you know, that physically aspect of being in a relationship is only a part of it. People have had distance relationships before - this will just be a very long-distance relationship.

NARRATION
After all, communication with the Mars base will still be possible, it just won't involve live chat, because the laws of physics mean there will always be a delay on any internet connection.

Bas Lansdorp
Imagine clicking your Google search for Mars and waiting for the signal to reach the Google server in San Francisco, which is 20 minutes, and then you wait for 20 minutes for your first 10 hits, then you click a hit and then the same thing happens again.

Dr Graham Phillips
My internet provider's not much better than that anyway.

(Bas chuckles)

NARRATION
And there are plenty of other challenges and risks getting to Mars. We have to work out how to farm food there, avoid the toxic Martian dust which is very high in thyroid-damaging chemicals, and some - who've perhaps read a bit too much science-fiction - even worry about catching Mars viruses.

Bas Lansdorp
I think the odds are very slim. We don't know if there's life on Mars at this moment so finding life, first of all, would be extremely exciting.

Dr Graham Phillips
'The good news is we've found life on Mars - the bad news is it's gonna kill you.'

NARRATION
One thing the astronauts will have to do is exploit the Martian resources, particularly the frozen water underground. So, surveying the planet in detail will be paramount. Andrew Dempster's team is helping to develop new kinds of satellites for space-surveying. They're called CubeSats.

Dr Graham Phillips
A regular satellite is about the size of a small car, but this new generation of CubeSats is that big, and they've still got all the key equipment - that's GPS, the orbit control, the power supply, communications - but all packed into a volume the size of two litres of milk.

NARRATION
Five test CubeSats were recently released from the International Space Station. Eventually, swarms of them will carry out space surveys of everything from asteroids to planets like Mars. A big, bold space future awaits us. But is our Martian dreaming really just an astronomical waste of money?

Dr Graham Phillips
Why not say, 'We've got enough problems here on Earth. We don't need to go to Mars.'

Bas Lansdorp
Politicians say, 'Well, every dollar spent on Apollo gave us $14 in return in economic value.' But I think that the most valuable thing that came from the Apollo missions were actually the pictures and the words and the stories and the videos. That's inspiration. And that's how kids get interested in pursuing a science career, that's how people get inspired to think big and to pursue their dreams.

Dr Graham Phillips
Yeah, I mean, it's a really interesting point of how many scientists were inspired by the Apollo landings. I wagged school for the day, basically, so I could watch it happen.

Neil Armstrong
That's one small step for man...

NARRATION
But Mars One has some very high hurdles to jump. For a start, they're still to raise the money from private investors. And their goal of a 2027 landing seems optimistic.

Professor Andrew Dempster
Mars One, as it's currently designed, will not succeed. But it's a starting point and there's no reason why, with a bit more work, it wouldn't be feasible.

Dianne McGrath
In marketing, we usually say, 'You set your goal in stone but your plan in sand.'

NARRATION
And for Dianne, the goal is very definitely set in red stone.

Dianne McGrath
There's something about the dreams we have as kids that we start to take on this yoke of responsibility as we grow up, and mortgages and houses and families. And why do we stop dreaming? I don't think we have to stop dreaming.

But I think that the most valuable thing that came from the Apollo missions were actually the pictures and the words and the stories and the videos. That's inspiration. And that's how kids get interested in pursuing a science career, that's how people get inspired to think big and to pursue their dreams. Dr Graham Phillips Yeah, I mean, it's a really interesting point of how many scientists were inspired by the Apollo landings. I wagged school for the day, basically, so I could watch it happen. Neil Armstrong That's one small step for man... NARRATION But Mars One has some very high hurdles to jump. For a start, they're still to raise the money from private investors. And their goal of a 2027 landing seems optimistic. Professor Andrew Dempster Mars One, as it's currently designed, will not succeed. But it's a starting point and there's no reason why, with a bit more work, it wouldn't be feasible. Dianne McGrath In marketing, we usually say, 'You set your goal in stone but your plan in sand.' NARRATION And for Dianne, the goal is very definitely set in red stone. Dianne McGrath There's something about the dreams we have as kids that we start to take on this yoke of responsibility as we grow up, and mortgages and houses and families. And why do we stop dreaming? I don't think we have to stop dreaming.
